newsitem.title: USA: US debt futures end lower, Hashimoto report cited.
newsitem.headline: US debt futures end lower, Hashimoto report cited.

text.p: U.S. debt futures ended lower, staging a late selloff after reported remarks by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto stoked fears that Japan would consider selling Treasurys to stabilize the yen.
A Market News Service report quoted Hashimoto as saying exchange rate stability was needed "so we will not be tempted to sell off U.S. Treasury bonds."
September Treasury bond futures fell to new session lows and the dollar eased back below 115.00 yen following Hashimoto's address at Columbia University in New York.

Until the final half-hour of trade, debt futures had maintained extremely tight ranges as a lack of fundamental factors kept players sidelined. The light volume made conditions ripe for an abrupt selloff, floor brokers said.
"We had a knee-jerk reaction behind some quotes late in the day," said a bond trader.
A Eurodollar trader attributed the swift drop in futures to a "liquidity trap" in the thin market.
Traders attributed light pressure on prices throughout the session to jitters before the two- and five-year Treasury note auctions get under way this week.
The Treasury will auction $15.5 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday, followed on Wednesday by $11.5 billion of five-year notes.
Some traders, believing the two-year note to be fairly priced at current levels, said the auction was having little impact on futures, based on the light order flows going through this session.
But other traders said the low yield on the note, at around 6.02 percent, would pose an obstacle to demand at the auction.
Arrival of the supply was keeping a lid on debt prices, which since April have been in an uptrend that shows no sign of reversing course, traders said.
"Once you get through the supply, you should see the market drift higher," said a Eurodollar broker for a Japanese bank.

U.S. June consumer confidence, also on Tuesday's agenda, is seen pulling back to 126.3 from 127.1 in May. The key report for the week, however, is May U.S. durable goods orders on Wednesday, traders said. Durables orders are expected up 0.6 percent versus 1.3 percent in April.
